rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: DSEAR requires employers to control safety risks from fire, explosions and substances corrosive to metals.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: DSEAR duties apply to employers and self-employed people and also protect members of the public put at risk by work activity.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Dangerous substances include solvents, paints, varnishes, LPG, combustible dusts, gases under pressure and substances corrosive to metal.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Employers must identify dangerous substances present in the workplace and assess the associated risks.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Employers must remove dangerous-substance risks where possible or otherwise put suitable control measures in place.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Controls must also reduce the consequences of incidents involving dangerous substances.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Plans and procedures must cover accidents, incidents and emergencies involving dangerous substances.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: Areas where explosive atmospheres may occur must be identified and classified, with ignition sources avoided in those areas.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: DSEAR risk depends on the substance, quantity, process, containment, ventilation, ignition sources, workforce and emergency arrangements.

rows.source: HSE dangerous substances and explosive atmospheres
rows.verified: HSE DSEAR guidance is workplace-, substance-, process-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire or explosion probability.
A COSHH assessment focuses on hazards and risks from hazardous substances in the workplace.
Harmful substances can be generated by work processes, including wood dust, silica dust and welding fumes.
Product labels and safety data sheets should be used to identify hazardous substances.
Assessment should consider inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion and other exposure routes.
Assessment should include maintenance workers, contractors, visitors and members of the public who could be exposed.
Elimination or substitution should be considered before relying on exposure controls.
Containment and local exhaust ventilation can reduce release of dust, fumes, mist, gases or vapour.
Workers must understand the assessment, exposure limits, controls, PPE requirements and emergency actions.
COSHH risk depends on the substance, concentration, route, duration, process, workforce, controls and maintenance condition.
COSHH assessment evidence is substance-, task-, worker-, exposure-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.
Workplaces need plans and practice for foreseeable hazardous-substance accidents, incidents and emergencies.
Emergency arrangements should include suitable equipment for spills and other foreseeable events.
Protective equipment and decontamination products should be available where the emergency plan requires them.
Procedures should cover how casualties will be dealt with.
People expected to act during an emergency must be trained for their roles.
Emergency arrangements should address safe handling and disposal of waste created by the incident.
Relevant emergency information should be made available to emergency services.
Employees and safety representatives should be involved and everyone should know the emergency plan.
Emergency effectiveness depends on the hazard, scenario, equipment, staffing, training, communications, access and response time.
COSHH emergency guidance is incident-, workplace-, substance-, responder-, equipment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level emergency outcome.
